lines.too_early: Good morning, I'm Dr. Okafor. Our shadowing session starts at 9:00, after your Pharmacodynamics lecture. Go to class first, then meet me right here.
lines.on_time: Right on time. That matters on the wards more than almost anything.
lines.late: You're a few minutes late. It happens, but on the wards being on time matters: the team rounds whether you're there or not. Let's get going.
lines.after: Good to see you again. 4 West is on Level 4; you know the way now. Keep those habits going.

stops.objective: Meet Dr. Okafor at the Information desk
stops.takeaway: Shadowing means observing: watch, listen, and save your questions for the right moment. The Information desk and the floor directories are how you find your way.

steps.say: Welcome to University Hospital. I'm one of the attending physicians on Internal Medicine, and you're with my team this morning.
Today you're shadowing. You watch, listen and ask good questions. You won't examine patients or write in the chart on your own; that comes later in your training.
Every hospital feels like a maze at first. The Information desk and the directories on each floor are your friends, and the elevators behind us serve every inpatient floor.
Our team is on 4 West, Internal Medicine. Stay close and follow me to the elevators.

stops.objective: Follow Dr. Okafor to the elevators
stops.takeaway: Elevators, hallways and the café are public spaces: no patient details there. Patients on beds and stretchers have priority in the elevators.

steps.say: Visitor elevators are here; the staff and patient-transport cars are at the end. If a patient on a bed or stretcher needs the car, they go first and we wait for the next one.
One rule for elevators, hallways and the café: they're public spaces.

steps.objective: Step into the elevator with Dr. Okafor

stops.takeaway: An inpatient unit is organized around its nurses station, with patient rooms along the corridors and the team workroom close by.

steps.say: Level 4: 4 West, Internal Medicine. Thirty-two beds; our team is caring for fourteen patients today.
Units are built around the nurses station, with patient rooms along the corridors and our workroom nearby. Let me show you.

stops.objective: Follow Dr. Okafor to the nurses station
stops.takeaway: The nurses station is the unit's hub. Introduce yourself to the charge nurse when you arrive; nurses coordinate the unit and spend the most time at the bedside.

steps.say: This is the nurses station, the hub of the unit. Nurses chart, take calls, watch the telemetry monitors and coordinate the day from here.
The board shows every room with its nurse, team and discharge plan. Nurses spend far more time at the bedside than we do; they often notice first when something changes.
Priya is our charge nurse today. It's good practice to introduce yourself whenever you arrive on a unit.

steps.objective: Introduce yourself to Priya, the charge nurse
steps.reply: Welcome to 4 West! If you ever lose your team, ask at the station. And please: clean hands, phone on silent.

stops.objective: Follow Dr. Okafor to the team workroom
stops.takeaway: The EHR is the shared record of notes, orders, results and medications. Chart review before rounds catches what changed; open only the charts you are involved with.

steps.say: Our team workroom. Before rounds we pre-round: we review each patient's chart so we know what changed overnight.
This is the electronic health record, the EHR. Every note, order, result and medication lives here, and the whole care team works from the same chart.
The banner at the top identifies the patient: name, age, room, allergies and code status. Always confirm you're in the right chart before you read anything.
Vital signs and their trends. Mr. Reyes in 412 came in with a fever; he has had a normal temperature for twenty-four hours.
Results. His white blood cell count is down from 14 to 11. New and abnormal results are flagged so they aren't missed.
Nursing and overnight notes tell the story between the numbers, and the orders and medication record show what is actually being done.

stops.takeaway: Before every room: read the door sign, knock, introduce yourself and clean your hands (foam in, foam out).

steps.say: Time to round on Mr. Reyes. Before any room: check the door for precaution signs, knock, and clean your hands.

steps.objective: Clean your hands at the dispenser beside room 412 (foam in)

steps.say: Exactly. Follow me in and stand at the foot of the bed.

stops.takeaway: On rounds the resident presents, the attending confirms the plan with the patient, and the student observes from the foot of the bed.

steps.objective: Stand at the foot of the bed

steps.say: Good morning, Mr. Reyes. This is a first-year medical student shadowing me today. Is it all right if they observe?

steps.speaker: patient
steps.say: Of course. Morning, Doc. I actually slept last night.

steps.speaker: martin
steps.say: Mr. Reyes is sixty-seven, admitted two days ago with community-acquired pneumonia. No fever for twenty-four hours, oxygen saturation ninety-five percent on room air, white count down to eleven.

steps.speaker: martin
steps.say: Plan: continue his antibiotics, walk twice today with nursing, and aim for discharge tomorrow if he keeps improving.
I agree. Mr. Reyes, what questions do you have for us?

steps.speaker: patient
steps.say: Just when I can go home.
If today goes like yesterday, tomorrow. We'll check in again this afternoon. Thank you.

steps.objective: Clean your hands on the way out (foam out)

stops.objective: Follow Dr. Okafor down the corridor
stops.takeaway: Read isolation signs before entering. Contact precautions: clean your hands, then gown and gloves, removed at the doorway.

steps.say: Look at the door of room 414. The yellow Contact Precautions sign means anyone going in needs a gown and gloves; the cart beside the door has them.
Different signs mean different equipment: contact, droplet, airborne. When in doubt, ask the patient's nurse before you go in.

stops.objective: Follow Dr. Okafor back toward the workroom
stops.takeaway: Be on time, silence your phone, observe without blocking, save questions for after the room, and thank the team.

steps.say: That's a morning on the floor. A few habits make a student welcome on any team.
Be on time. Phone on silent. Stand where you can see without blocking anyone. Save your questions for after we leave the room, then ask all of them.
And thank the nurses on your way out. You did well today. Come back to 4 West any time; you know the way now.
